title: Zscaler Sets a $10 Billion ARR Target and Wall Street Stays Skeptical
subtitle: Management mapped out a five-year path to triple its business, but a lagging valuation multiple reveals deep skepticism about seat-based growth.
summary: Zscaler reaffirmed its near-term forecast while projecting a long-term run to as much as $10 billion in annual recurring revenue. The cloud security pioneer still trades at a fraction of its peers' sales multiples as investors debate whether AI agents will expand its market or eat its core pricing model.

bodyHtml:
When an enterprise software leader promises to nearly triple its business over the next five years, Wall Street usually throws a parade.

The Numbers That Matter
Price LIVE$220.43
Market Cap$35.5B
Forward P/E38.74
Total Revenue (TTM)$3.35B
52-Week Low$114.62
52-Week High$336.99
Analyst ConsensusBuy (44 analysts)
Analyst Target Mean$233.38
Price refreshes live. All other figures as of October 15, 2026.

At its first investor day in five years, Zscaler mapped out a long-term path for its annual recurring revenue. The base case calls for more than $8 billion by fiscal 2031, with an upside target of $10 billion against roughly $3.8 billion today.

Yet while peers like CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks have roughly doubled or better over the past year, Zscaler has spent the cycle stuck in neutral. The stock lost about two-thirds of its value between late 2025 and its spring 2026 low, and the broader cybersecurity rally has largely left it behind.

To understand why the market is hesitating, you have to look at what Zscaler actually sells. Think of the traditional corporate network like an office building with a locked front door. Once your badge scans you through the lobby, you can wander into any conference room, break room, or executive suite.

Zscaler threw out the front door entirely. Its cloud platform sits directly between a company's staff and the web, forcing every single click, application, and file request to prove its identity individually before granting access. Over 11,000 corporate customers—including more than 40% of the Fortune 500—rely on this architecture to keep employees from infecting company systems or leaking sensitive files.

That gatekeeper role is becoming vital for the artificial intelligence buildout.

When autonomous software agents start writing code, pulling spreadsheets, and pinging internal databases, they do not sit at a desk with a laptop or an enterprise Slack account. They act like tireless digital workers that need strict identity checks and egress rules so proprietary internal records do not slip into public training models.

Security for AI is generating roughly $70 million in recurring revenue and data security has topped $400 million, positioning the platform to secure machine traffic just as it secured human browsers. CEO Jay Chaudhry calls the agentic-AI wave "quickly becoming the most significant opportunity in our company's history."

The financial disconnect is what makes the setup compelling. Zscaler closed out fiscal 2026 growing revenue 25% to $3.35 billion, matching the top-line pace of CrowdStrike almost point for point.

Yet Zscaler trades at less than a quarter of CrowdStrike's sales multiple and commands a deep discount to Palo Alto Networks. The company expanded its total addressable market estimate to $220 billion, up from $62 billion when it focused strictly on human workers. On paper, investors are getting top-tier cloud security growth at a bargain valuation.

Short sellers will tell you that the discount is not an oversight; it is an eviction notice. Management merely reaffirmed fiscal 2027 revenue growth of roughly 17%, confirming a sharp step-down from the 25% pace that triggered a brutal 31% single-day stock plunge when first signaled in May.

Strip out the acquisition of Red Canary, and fiscal 2026 organic revenue grew 20%, with organic net new annual recurring revenue coming in at just 14%. Cash conversion is also bleeding, with free cash flow margins dropping to 23% for the full year and sliding to just 7% in the fourth quarter as data center spending surged.

More threatening is the pricing model: the bulk of Zscaler's contracts bill per human seat, and if autonomous software agents replace office workers rather than augment them, those seats disappear. If first-quarter net new recurring revenue lands below management's 15% full-year marker, the bears will be proven right.

For the equity to re-rate, Zscaler does not need to invent magic; it needs to show that the growth deceleration has found a floor. Bulls point to the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, where organic net new recurring revenue growth accelerated to 17% from just 7% a year earlier.

Non-seat solutions—which price based on data, cloud workloads, and branch offices—doubled their recurring revenue over the past year and now account for nearly a third of new contract value. If those non-seat offerings continue scaling fast enough to neutralize the per-seat drag while capital spending cools, the multiple discount should narrow.

The immediate test arrives with the first-quarter print, where net new recurring revenue must deliver roughly 15% of the full-year target to confirm the recovery is real. Until then, the promise of ten billion dollars in recurring revenue remains just a slide deck.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in ZS. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
